rv.q: The acrobatics of love are performed in high style in “Brief Encounter,” which is surely the most enchanting work of stagecraft ever inspired by a movie.
Now Ms. Rice and her wonderful company have made it possible to embrace "Brief Encounter" once more with feeling, and without irony or embarrassment.
It's a spirited charm offensive that's just impossible to resist.
We roll along with them, enchanted.

Upon entering the theater, you're greeted by ushers in period garb who regale you with comic banter and musical numbers. This immersion continues with the show proper, which ingeniously incorporates old-style film images and projections into which the characters pop in and out.
Even so, strict devotees of the film might feel that their favorite has been trivialized by a cascade of songs and laughs.
Rice finds too much of herself and too little of Coward. She deploys his plot and his songs, but her ironic flashiness illustrates rather than penetrates the punishing emotions of the film.
Work as imaginative and wholly successful as "Brief Encounter" doesn't come along every day.
In 1945, master imp and conscientious keeper-of-British-values Noel Coward adapted his one-act Still Life into Brief Encounter, the seminal stiff-upper-lip-tearjerker film now beloved by millions.
Emma Rice’s 90 minute encounter with Noel Coward’s great work -- equally sublime -- stands on its own.
Even if you're not familiar with David Lean's 1946 movie melodrama Brief Encounter, you will find yourself caught up in writer-director Emma Rice's brilliantly reconceived stage adaptation.
“Brief Encounter” is a contagious evening of theater.
Call me impatient, but it was too long to wait in this "Brief" affair.
But what's missing is the movie's emotional core the impassioned delicacy of its portrayal of two people who glimpse all too briefly the romance that their ordinary lives can never permit.
The result is a hash that neither honors the original nor justifies spoofing it at such length.
If you want to have a very good time, go to this production.
The end result is just as clever as it is irritating and unnecessary.
This show annoyed me greatly—as I watched it and then, later, as I thought about what it signified.

cn.t: Critics are charmed by this inventive British adaptation's theatrical ingenuity and playful stagecraft, though some find the quirky multimedia approach undermines Coward's emotional core. Most praise its enchanting wit; detractors call it gimmicky.
